hook.support: A form comes back with a red stamp: **RETURNED**. You missed one box. Now you wait another two weeks. Most mistakes on forms are easy to stop.
hook.core: Your form comes back with a sticky note: **“Incomplete. Please resubmit.”** One empty box, and you’re back in the queue. Forms aren’t hard. They’re just strict. Read them the right way and you get it right the first time.
hook.extend: A form is a contract with a set of rules. Miss one box, use the wrong date format or sign in the wrong place, and an application for a licence, a job, a concession or a course can bounce back weeks later. The fix isn’t speed. It’s reading the instructions first and checking before you sign.

why.support: You’ll fill in forms for jobs, Medicare, TAFE, your licence and more. Getting them right saves time and money.
why.core: Jobs, TAFE, Medicare, your licence, a bank account, a sports club: they all start with a form. Getting it right the first time saves weeks of waiting, and sometimes money.
why.extend: Forms are how organisations decide who gets a service, a job or a payment. Accurate, complete forms get processed; incomplete ones get delayed or rejected. It’s a skill you’ll use for the rest of your life.

articles.title: Forms are strict, not hard

body.support:
Forms are not hard. They are **strict**. Follow four steps.

1. **Read it all first.** Look at every page. Read the instructions at the top.
2. **Gather what you need.** Get your ID, card numbers and dates ready.
3. **Follow its rules.**
   - Use **BLOCK LETTERS** if it asks.
   - Write the date the way it asks. In Australia, it’s usually day, then month, then year: 04/09/2009.
   - Fill in every box marked **\***. It means **required**.
   - If a question doesn’t apply, write **N/A** (not applicable).
   - “If no, go to question 8” means skip ahead.
4. **Check, then sign.** Check every box. Then sign and date it. Keep a copy or a photo.
body.core:
Forms aren’t hard. They’re **strict**. A form is checked by someone (or a computer) looking for anything missing or wrong. Four steps get it right the first time.

1. **Read it all first.** Skim every page before you write a word. Read the instructions at the top and any notes in small print. Look for words like “must”, “required” and “attach”.
2. **Gather what you need.** Most forms want ID (like a birth certificate, passport or student card), numbers (Medicare, tax file number, a reference number) and dates. Get them on the table first.
3. **Follow its rules.**
   - **BLOCK LETTERS** and **black pen** if it asks.
   - Dates the way it asks. In Australia, it’s usually **DD/MM/YYYY**: day, month, year.
   - Every box marked **\*** is **required**. Leave one blank and it can come back.
   - Write **N/A** (not applicable) if a question doesn’t apply, so they know you didn’t miss it.
   - Follow skip instructions: “If No, go to Question 8.”
   - Don’t write in boxes marked **Office use only**.
4. **Check, then sign.** Check every box against your ID. Read the **declaration**: you’re promising it’s true. Then sign and date it, last. Keep a copy or a photo.

Long instructions? Turn them into a numbered list of steps before you start. It’s much easier to follow.
body.extend:
Forms aren’t hard. They’re **strict**. Every form is checked against a set of rules, by a person or a system, and anything missing, unclear or inconsistent can send it back. Four steps get it right the first time.

1. **Read it all first.** Skim every page before writing anything, then read the instructions closely. Scan for signal words: *must*, *required*, *attach*, *only if*.
2. **Gather what you need.** Identity documents, reference numbers (Medicare, tax file number, a customer number), dates and addresses. Information that doesn’t match your ID exactly is a common reason for delay.
3. **Follow its rules.**
   - **BLOCK LETTERS** and **black pen** where asked.
   - Dates in the stated format; in Australia usually **DD/MM/YYYY**.
   - Complete every **required** field (often marked **\***).
   - Write **N/A** where a question doesn’t apply, so the assessor knows you saw it.
   - Follow skip logic (“If No, go to Question 8”).
   - Leave **Office use only** sections blank.
4. **Check, then sign.** Check each field against your documents, read the **declaration** (a legal promise that the information is true), then sign and date it last. Keep a copy.

Unfamiliar form words often break into parts you know: *applicant* is the person who *applies*; *residential* comes from *reside*, to live. And long instructions are easier to follow if you first summarise them as a short, numbered list of steps.

caseStudies.title: The votes that didn’t count

body.support:
Voting is a form too. For the House of Representatives, you must number **every** box, in order.

At the 2022 federal election, **5.19%** of House of Representatives votes didn’t count. That’s about **1 in 20**. These are called **informal** votes.

In two seats in Sydney, Blaxland and Fowler, more than **10%** didn’t count.

People counting the votes in Fowler said many voters had not filled in all the boxes.

Most of these people wanted to vote. A small form mistake meant their vote was lost.
body.core:
Your ballot paper is a form, and it has strict rules. For the House of Representatives, you must number **every** box, in order of who you prefer.

At the 2022 federal election, the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) counted **5.19%** of House of Representatives votes as **informal**. That means they didn’t count. It’s about one vote in twenty.

In some seats, it was much higher. In Blaxland and Fowler, in western Sydney, more than **10%** of House votes were informal.

Scrutineers (people who watch the count) in Fowler told SBS News that many voters had failed to fill out all the squares. Experts also pointed to language barriers and confusion about how preferential voting works.

Most of these voters weren’t trying to waste their vote. A form rule they didn’t understand cost them their say.
body.extend:
A ballot paper is one of the most important forms you’ll ever fill in, and it’s strict. For the House of Representatives, a vote only counts if every box is numbered in order of preference.

At the 2022 federal election, the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) recorded **5.19%** of House of Representatives votes as **informal**: about one in twenty. In the western Sydney seats of Blaxland and Fowler, the rate was more than **10%**.

Scrutineers in Fowler told SBS News that many voters had not filled out every square. Most had not left the paper blank on purpose. Experts pointed to language barriers, too little community outreach, and confusion about preferential voting. Analysts have also noticed that informal votes tend to rise when there are more candidates on the ballot.

The lesson reaches well beyond elections. When a form’s rules aren’t clear to the people filling it in, good intentions get lost. Reading the instructions, and helping others understand them, matters.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** NGUYEN — accepted; 9/4/09 — sent back (format, year); blank phone — sent back (required); N/A middle name — accepted; signed with no date — sent back; writing in office-use box — sent back.

**Annotation:** 1 instructions (black pen, block letters, * required); 2 required fields in block letters; 3 date format DD/MM/YYYY; 4 “same as above”; 5 skip instruction (No → Q8); 6 declaration, sign and date last.

**Steps (example):** 1 Fill in all sections in black pen and block letters. 2 If under 18, get a parent or guardian to sign Section D. 3 Attach a copy of one photo ID. 4 Return it in person or scan and email it. 5 Wait up to 10 business days for the pass in the post.

**Case study:** an informal vote doesn’t count; many voters didn’t number every box; better translated information, outreach and clear instructions could help.

realityCheck: **Privacy first.** Real forms contain Medicare numbers, TFNs and addresses. Never collect them; students show forms with private details covered, and nothing is photocopied for the class.
**Some students won’t have a form they need right now.** Keep a set of real blank forms (library, sport, work experience) so everyone can do a real one.
**Don’t make students submit forms they don’t want.** The skill is completing it correctly; submitting is their choice (or a parent’s, for under-18s).
**Online forms count.** Many are now online only; students can screenshot each page instead of printing.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It’s short and immediately useful, and students often bring forms from home once they see it.
